## How rehydra differs from existing packages

Resistance, recovery and resilience indices are not new to R. `pointRes`
implements the components of Lloret et al. (2011) and has been the reference
implementation for well over a decade. `rehydra` uses the same three ratios as
its starting point, and deliberately so: an index that disagrees with the
established definition would be a liability, not a feature. The two packages
nevertheless answer different questions, because they were built for different
kinds of data.

`pointRes` was written for **dendrochronology**. Its unit of observation is the
annual growth ring, its unit of disturbance is the pointer year, and the whole
design follows from that: one value per tree per year, disturbances identified
retrospectively from the chronology, and resilience components computed from a
window of years before and after the event.

`rehydra` was written for **controlled drought-rewatering experiments on live
plants**. The unit of observation is a physiological measurement taken during an
experiment the researcher designed, and every difference below follows from that
change of scale.

### Physiological variables instead of ring width

Ring width is a single, always-positive, always-"more-is-better" variable.
Ecophysiology is not so accommodating. `rehydra` is built around chlorophyll
fluorescence (`Fv/Fm`, `PhiPSII`, `NPQ`), leaf water potential, stomatal
conductance, net photosynthesis, transpiration and derived water-use efficiency
terms — measured in the same experiment, on different scales, and pointing in
different directions.

Leaf water potential is the awkward case that motivates the design: it is
negative, and *more negative is worse*. Feeding it to a ratio index unchanged
produces a resistance value that is confidently backwards. `prepare_rehydra_data()`
therefore carries an explicit `response_direction` for every variable, and can
infer it from the variable name:

```r
library(rehydra)
data(rehydra_data)

prepared <- prepare_rehydra_data(
  data = rehydra_data,
  time = time_days,
  genotype = genotype,
  treatment = treatment,
  replicate = replicate,
  variables = c(water_potential, stomatal_conductance),
  response_direction = "auto"
)
```

The `transformed_value` column that comes out is on a consistent
"higher is better", strictly positive performance scale, which is the only scale
on which the ratio indices `Rt`, `Rc` and `Rs` mean what their definitions say
they mean.

### Daily and sub-daily resolution instead of annual

A tree ring gives one number per year. A porometer gives one number per plant per
hour, and a fluorimeter can give many more. That extra resolution is not just
more of the same data — it makes a different class of index computable.

With one value per year you can only ask *how far* the response fell and *how far*
it came back. With a densely sampled trajectory you can also ask *how fast*, *in
what shape*, and *after how long a delay*. `curve_shape_metrics()` reads those
off the whole series:

- **area under the deficit curve** — the integral of `max(0, baseline − y(t))`,
  the total performance lost, evaluated by the trapezoidal rule so that irregular
  sampling is handled correctly;
- **`t50`** — the interpolated time to close half of the gap, with finer
  resolution than the sampling interval;
- **`recovery_rate_k`** — the rate constant of the exponential return, fitted by
  nonlinear least squares from a log-linear starting value;
- **`latency`** — the delay between restoring water and the first measurable
  upturn, which for hydraulic variables is routinely positive and is invisible to
  any endpoint-based index.

Two plants can share an identical `Rs` and differ completely in all four. The
whole point of sub-daily data is to be able to tell them apart.

### Multiple cycles in one experiment, with explicit segmentation

`pointRes` identifies disturbances retrospectively, from the statistical
structure of the chronology. In a designed experiment the researcher *imposed*
the cycles and knows when they happened.

`segment_drought_cycle()` supports both. In `method = "manual"` the known
irrigation calendar is supplied directly and the segmentation is exact. In
`method = "auto"` the phases are detected from smoothed trajectories, first
derivatives and relative drop/recovery thresholds, each cycle receiving a
`confidence` score; when detection is not confident the function says so rather
than returning a quiet guess. Either way the output labels every observation with
a `cycle` and one of `PreDrought`, `Drought`, `Rewatering`, `PostDrought`, so a
three-cycle experiment yields three fully separated cycles in one table instead
of three separate analyses that must be stitched together by hand.

### Experimental design as a first-class citizen

This is the largest structural difference. A dendrochronological package has
trees and sites. An experimental package has genotypes, treatments, blocks,
plots, pots, replicates and a randomization — and the indices are *responses* in
that design, not the end of the analysis.

`rehydra_anova()` fits the randomized-complete-block factorial model the design
implies, on any index the package computes:

```r
segments <- segment_drought_cycle(prepared, time = time, value = transformed_value)
res <- resilience_index(segments)

fit <- rehydra_anova(
  res,
  response = "Rs",
  factors = c("genotype", "treatment")
)
fit$anova
fit$comparisons
```

It returns the ANOVA table, marginal means whose standard errors come from the
**pooled residual error** of the model rather than from within-cell standard
deviations, all pairwise Tukey contrasts, and normality and homogeneity
diagnostics. One model is fitted per variable and per cycle, because repeated
cycles measured on the same plants are not independent and a single model
treating cycle as another crossed factor would understate the standard errors.

When the cycles should be modelled jointly, the dependence goes into the model
rather than being ignored:

```r
rehydra_anova(res, response = "Rs",
              factors = c("genotype", "treatment", "cycle"),
              by = "variable", random = "plant_id")
```

Every reported table then comes from the mixed model, and
`diagnostics$model_type` and `diagnostics$p_value_method` record which model and
which degrees of freedom produced them.

Two more design tools have no counterpart in a dendrochronological package
because they only make sense for an experiment someone is about to run or has
just run: `memory_power()` computes the replication needed to detect a given
between-cycle effect from the non-central t distribution, with paired and
independent designs, and `memory_power_pilot()` extracts the residual standard
deviation and the between-cycle correlation from a pilot to feed it.

### Between-cycle memory indices

Nothing in `pointRes` asks whether a tree that survived one drought handles the
next one better, because with annual resolution and retrospective disturbance
detection the question is very hard to pose. In an experiment with an imposed
sequence of cycles it is the central question, and it is the concept `rehydra`
was built around.

`memory_effect()` contrasts cycles pairwise:

```r
memory <- memory_effect(res, cycle_ref = 1, cycle_test = 2)
memory[, c("genotype", "Mem_Rt", "Mem_Rc", "Mem_Rs", "interpretation")]
```

`memory_trend()` fits the whole sequence when there are three or more cycles,
returning the **memory rate** — the average change in an index per additional
cycle — with its confidence interval, p-value and a `monotonic_fraction` that
exposes a slope driven by one anomalous cycle rather than by a consistent
progression:

```r
memory_trend(res, min_cycles = 2)
```

And `priming_classification()` turns the numbers into the categories
physiologists actually report: `positive_priming`, `negative_priming`,
`neutral_memory`, `overcompensation`, `incomplete_recovery`, `maladaptation`.

The direction of "better" is handled automatically. For damage-type indices
(`deficit_auc`, `total_reduction`, `mean_reduction`, `t50`, `residual_deficit`)
a falling value means the plant coped better, so `memory_trend()` flips the sign
before labelling and `"acquired_memory"` always means the same thing regardless
of which index it describes. `memory_direction()` exposes that mapping.

### A superset of the published index families

`rehydra` implements the Lloret components and adds the families that describe
duration, average intensity and curve shape, so that a study does not have to
choose one summary of the episode:

| Family | Function | Indices |
|---|---|---|
| Lloret et al. (2011) | `resilience_index()` | `Rt`, `Rc`, `Rs` |
| Duration and total loss | `recovery_period_metrics()` | `recovery_period`, `total_reduction` |
| Average intensity and rate | `mean_reduction_metrics()` | `mean_reduction`, `mean_recovery_rate` |
| Curve shape | `curve_shape_metrics()` | `deficit_auc`, `t50`, `recovery_rate_k`, `latency` |
| Stability | `overall_stability()` | `impact`, `disturbance_rate`, `recovery_rate`, `OSt` |
| Memory | `memory_effect()`, `memory_trend()` | `Mem_*`, memory rate, priming class |
| All of them | `rehydra_indices()` | every family joined on one key |

All five families read the same five landmarks — baseline, stress onset,
rewatering onset, trough, series end — extracted once by a shared internal
routine. They therefore cannot disagree about where the trough or the baseline
is, which is what makes the indices comparable to each other within a single
analysis.

Two details that matter for honest reporting are handled explicitly.
`recovery_period` is **right-censored** when the series ends before the response
returns to the recovery threshold: it is reported as `NA` with
`recovery_censored = TRUE`, not silently truncated to the length of the
experiment, which would make the slowest genotypes look like the fastest. And
`stress_detected` flags cycles whose trough never left the baseline — control
series, or a stress too mild to register — so those rows can be filtered instead
of being averaged in as if they were recoveries.

### One score across variables

Because several variables are measured in the same experiment,
`composite_resilience()` collapses an index across them into a single score, by
PCA, by an unweighted mean or with weights decided a priori:

```r
score <- composite_resilience(res, metric = "Rs")
composite_loadings(score)
```

The `variance_explained` that comes back is the point of using PCA here rather
than a plain average: a first component explaining 0.8 means the variables
largely agree and one score is a fair summary, while 0.4 means they disagree and
the composite is hiding a trade-off that belongs in the results per variable.

### Sub-daily rhythms

The resolution that makes curve-shape indices possible also brings a problem a
yearly series never has: stomatal conductance and photosynthesis swing more
between dawn and midday than the drought moves them, so a trough detected on the
raw series can be noon. `detrend_diurnal()` separates the two, estimating the
daily rhythm jointly with an across-days component so that the multi-day drought
course is preserved rather than partly absorbed into the daily wave:

```r
hourly <- detrend_diurnal(prepared, time = timestamp)
segment_drought_cycle(hourly, time = time, value = detrended)
```

### In short

| | `pointRes` | `rehydra` |
|---|---|---|
| Data | Annual ring width | Physiological time series |
| Resolution | Yearly | Daily / sub-daily |
| Disturbance | Detected retrospectively | Imposed and segmented |
| Cycles | One event at a time | Several cycles per experiment |
| Design | Trees and sites | Genotype, treatment, block, replicate |
| Inference | Index summaries | ANOVA, marginal means, Tukey contrasts |
| Memory | Not addressed | Pairwise and multi-cycle memory indices |
| Repeated measures | Not applicable | Mixed model across cycles |
| Multiple variables | One (ring width) | Combined into a composite score |
| Sub-daily rhythms | Not applicable | Diurnal detrending |
| Planning | Not addressed | Power and replication for a memory effect |
| Interface | R only | R plus a bundled Shiny application |

The packages are complements, not competitors. Analysing tree-ring chronologies
is what `pointRes` is for. Analysing a designed drought-rewatering experiment on
live plants, at physiological resolution, across repeated cycles, is what
`rehydra` is for.

## References

- Lloret, F., Keeling, E. G., Sala, A. (2011) <doi:10.1111/j.1600-0706.2011.19372.x>
- Xu, Z., Zhou, G., Shimizu, H. (2010) <doi:10.4161/psb.5.6.11398>
- Ribeiro et al. (2021) <doi:10.1016/j.jplph.2021.153397>

Run `rehydra_references()` for the machine-readable version, including which
DOIs have been verified as resolvable.

The recovery-period, total-reduction, mean-reduction and mean-recovery-rate
components carry no citation on purpose. They are generic quantities - time to
return to baseline, cumulative loss, average deficit, average rate - and their
exact definitions are given as mathematics in `?recovery_period_metrics` and
`?mean_reduction_metrics`. Attributing them to a work that could not be verified
would be worse than describing precisely what is computed.
